```python
    'y ~ Q_incent + Q_reorg + EntityEffects + TimeEffects',
    data=df.set_index(['worker_task', 't'])
).fit()

tau_incent_hat = fe.params['Q_incent']
tau_reorg_hat  = fe.params['Q_reorg']
```

---

## The killer feature — bias against known truth

The ABM sets $\tau_{\text{incent}}^{\text{structural}}$ and $\tau_{\text{reorg}}^{\text{structural}}$ inside the simulation. After each strategy, compute:

$$\text{bias}_{s} \;=\; \hat\tau_{s} - \tau^{\text{structural}}$$

Typical output:

| Strategy | Assumption tested | $\hat\tau_{\text{incent}}$ | truth | bias | $\hat\tau_{\text{reorg}}$ | truth | bias |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1. 2×2** | Random assignment | 20.1% | 20% | +0.1% ✅ | 8.2% | 8% | +0.2% ✅ |
| **2. Staged** | Stable incentive across phases | 20.0% | 20% | 0% ✅ | 7.5% | 8% | −0.5% ✅ |
| **3. FE** | Task-switch exogenous \| FE | 22.3% | 20% | +2.3% ⚠️ | 9.6% | 8% | +1.6% ⚠️ |
| **Naive DiD** | none | 33% | 20% | +13% ❌ | — | — | — |

---

## Stress-test the strategies inside the ABM

Because you control the DGP, break assumptions and re-run:

```python
scenarios = [
    'baseline',
    'endogenous_task_switching',   # managers move stars first
    'learning_by_doing',           # workers improve with tenure
    'peer_spillovers',             # SUTVA violated
    'compliance_15pct',            # 15% of teams deviate from RCT protocol
]

for scenario in scenarios:
    for strategy in [S1, S2, S3]:
        biases[scenario, strategy] = run_and_estimate(scenario, strategy)
```

Produces a **bias grid**: which strategy survives which threat.

| Scenario | Strategy 1 bias | Strategy 2 bias | Strategy 3 bias |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | ~0% | ~0% | ~2% |
| + endogenous switching | ~0% | ~0% | **+8%** ⚠️ |
| + learning by doing | ~0% | +2% (contamination) | +5% |
| + peer spillovers | +3% (SUTVA) | +3% | +4% |
| + 15% non-compliance | ~0% (ITT) | +5% | +6% |

**Report to Quindi**: "In your typical client environment, use Strategy 1 if possible (biases < 3% under all threats). If Strategy 3 is your only option, expect +5–8% upward bias on $\hat\tau_{\text{incent}}$; report confidence intervals accordingly."

---

## What the ABM gives you that empirical work cannot

| Quantity | Empirical | ABM |
|---|---|---|
| True $\tau_{\text{incent}}$, $\tau_{\text{reorg}}$ | **Unknown** | **Known (set in config)** |
| Bias of estimator | **Unknown** (no ground truth) | **Directly measurable** |
| Sensitivity to confounders | Requires natural experiment | Set them on/off in config |
| Power calculations | Simulate under assumed effect | Simulate under known effect |
| Interaction effects | Requires 2×2 in real world | Trivial: cell (1,1) − others |

The ABM's *identification purpose* is to tell Quindi **which empirical strategy to invest in for each client**, and by how much each strategy would lie in that client's specific environment.

---

### References

- **Neugart & Richiardi (2018)** — ABM validation patterns.
- **Manski (2003, 2007)** — partial identification bounds (useful when strategies give conflicting estimates).
- **Chesher (2010)** — instrumental identification in structural models.
- **Athey & Imbens (2017, JEP)** — the state of applied econometrics — ML meets causal inference.
- **Bertrand, Duflo, Mullainathan (2004)** — clustered SE for panel DiD.

→ Anchor: **ABM Theory Core**

nodes.title: ★ Optimal Quindi Reward Formula
nodes.content:
# Optimal Quindi Reward Formula

## Umbrella frame (Holmström–Milgrom 1987)

> Under CARA + Gaussian noise, the optimal linear contract is $w = \alpha + \beta \cdot s$, where $s$ is a **signal vector**. Piece rates = a specific $(\beta, s)$; tournaments = ranking-based $s$; profit share = team $s$. The design choice is **what signal $s$** you contract on and **whose $s$** (self, peer, team, firm).

## Signal vector for Quindi

Four signals, each targeting a distinct failure family:

| # | Signal | Definition | Whose | Fixes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $s_3$ | Peer-relative combined index (quantity + quality) | $[q_i - \bar q_{\text{peers}}] + \lambda [Q_i - \bar Q_{\text{peers}}]$ | Self vs peers | **F1**, **F2**, **F3** |
| $s_4$ | Cooperation signal | mentoring hits, help-given, knowledge-share flags | Self + peer-reported | **F5**, **F7** |
| $s_5$ | Team output | small-team KPI ($N \approx 5$) | Team | **F5**, **F7** |
| $s_6$ | Subjective manager rating | manager's assessment | Manager | **F1**, **F2**, **F6** |

Definitions:
- $q_i$ = individual throughput (calls closed, tickets resolved),
- $Q_i$ = individual quality (CSAT, error rate, rework),
- $\bar q_{\text{peers}}, \bar Q_{\text{peers}}$ = peer-group means,
- $\lambda > 0$ = relative price of quality vs quantity.

## Contract

$$\boxed{\; w_i \;=\; \alpha \;+\; \beta_3\, s_{3}(i) \;+\; \beta_4\, s_{4}(i) \;+\; \beta_5\, s_{5} \;+\; \beta_6\, s_{6}(i) \;}$$

Unpacked:

$$
w_i \;=\; \underbrace{\alpha}_{\text{floor (F4)}} + \underbrace{\beta_3 \big[(q_i - \bar q_{\text{peers}}) + \lambda (Q_i - \bar Q_{\text{peers}})\big]}_{\text{peer-relative Q+Q, F1/F2/F3}} + \underbrace{\beta_4\, s_{4}(i)}_{\text{cooperation, F5}} + \underbrace{\beta_5\, s_{5}}_{\text{team share, F5/F7}} + \underbrace{\beta_6\, s_{6}(i)}_{\text{subjective, F1/F2/F6}}
$$

## Optimal weight vector $\boldsymbol{\beta}^{*}$

From Holmström–Milgrom (1991) multitasking:

$$\boxed{\; \boldsymbol{\beta}^{*} \;=\; \big(I + \rho\, C\, \Sigma\big)^{-1}\, \mathbf{g}' \;}$$

where $\boldsymbol{\beta} = (\beta_3, \beta_4, \beta_5, \beta_6)^\top$ and
- $\mathbf{g}' = (\partial V / \partial e_j)_{j\in\{3,4,5,6\}}$ — marginal firm value of effort on each dim,
- $C$ — effort-cost Hessian ($4 \times 4$),
- $\Sigma$ — noise covariance of $(s_3, s_4, s_5, s_6)$,
- $\rho$ — CARA risk aversion of workforce.

**Reading it**:
- $\Sigma_{jj} \uparrow$ (noisier signal) $\Rightarrow \beta_j^{*} \downarrow$: don't pay heavily on noisy signals.
- Off-diagonal $\Sigma_{jk} > 0$ (correlated) $\Rightarrow$ down-weight the noisier of the pair.
- $\rho \uparrow$ (risk-averse) $\Rightarrow$ all $\beta_j^{*} \downarrow$: shift toward fixed pay $\alpha$.

**Balance condition** (no dimension arbitrable):

$$\frac{\beta_j^{*}}{\beta_k^{*}} \;=\; \frac{g_j' / (1 + \rho\,\sigma_j^2\, k_j / g_j'^{\,2})}{g_k' / (1 + \rho\,\sigma_k^2\, k_k / g_k'^{\,2})}$$

## Optimal $\lambda^{*}$

Set $\lambda$ so quantity and quality generate equal marginal firm value:

$$\lambda^{*} \;=\; \frac{\partial V / \partial Q}{\partial V / \partial q}$$

## Estimating parameters from Quindi data

- **$\sigma_j^2$** — residual variance of $s_j$ after netting worker fixed effects.
- **$\rho$** — risk-preference survey OR back out via WTA in current pay.
- **$k_j = c_{jj}''$** — labor-supply elasticity: within-worker effort response to bonus variation.
- **$g_j'$** — firm-level regression $V = \sum_j g_j'\, s_j + \varepsilon$.

With $(\rho, \Sigma, C, \mathbf{g}', \lambda)$ estimated, $\boldsymbol\beta^{*}$ is a closed-form matrix computation.

## What this contract accomplishes

| Failure | Fixed via |
|---|---|
| **F1** measurement | $s_3$ peer-relative (common shock cancelled) + $s_6$ subjective correction |
| **F2** multitasking | Balanced $\boldsymbol\beta$ across all 4 dims, incl. $\lambda$ in $s_3$ |
| **F3** ratchet | $s_3$ peer-indexed, not history-indexed |
| **F4** risk transfer | Floor $\alpha$ + HM-optimal $\|\boldsymbol\beta\|$ |
| **F5**, **F7** cooperation | $s_4$ + $s_5$ directly price the externality (offset the peer-relative sabotage risk of $s_3$) |
| **F6** Goodhart | Multi-dim + subjective override — no single kink to game |
| **A9** selection | Structure attracts cooperative, quality-oriented types ex-ante |

## Implication for the ATE study

Use the composite outcome

$$R_i \;=\; \boldsymbol\beta^{*\top}\, \mathbf{s}_i \;=\; \beta_3^{*} s_{3}(i) + \beta_4^{*} s_{4}(i) + \beta_5^{*} s_{5} + \beta_6^{*} s_{6}(i)$$

$$\hat\tau \;=\; \bar R_{T=1} - \bar R_{T=0}$$

$\hat\tau$ is (i) invariant to intra-worker task reallocation, (ii) cooperation-aware (via $s_4, s_5$), (iii) noise-optimal (via $\Sigma$-weighting), (iv) filters common shocks (via $s_3$'s peer-relative form).

**Cautions**
- **Peer group definition**: if AI treatment is uneven across peers, $s_3$ contaminates. Fix: define peer group at untreated baseline OR use saturation design.
- **SUTVA / spillovers**: $s_5$ team component embeds treatment spillover — use saturation design to identify direct vs spillover effects.

## Bottom line

Four signals $(s_3, s_4, s_5, s_6)$, four weights $(\beta_3, \beta_4, \beta_5, \beta_6)$, plus $\alpha$ and $\lambda$. $R_i = \boldsymbol\beta^{*\top}\mathbf{s}_i$ is Quindi's evaluation index AND the outcome variable of the ATE study.

---

### References

- **Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1987)**. Aggregation and linearity in the provision of intertemporal incentives. *Econometrica*, 55(2), 303–328 (linear contract).
- **Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1991)**. Multitask principal–agent analyses. *JLEO*, 7(Special), 24–52 (matrix formula).
- **Baker, G. (1992)**. Incentive contracts and performance measurement. *JPE*, 100(3), 598–614 (signal-selection theory).
- **Feltham, G. & Xie, J. (1994)**. Performance measure congruity and diversity. *Accounting Review*, 69(3), 429–453.
- **Holmström, B. (1982)**. Moral hazard in teams. *Bell JE*, 13, 324–340 (peer benchmark / team component).
- **Shleifer, A. (1985)**. A theory of yardstick competition. *RAND JE*, 16(3), 319–327.
- **MacLeod, W. B. (2003)**. Optimal contracting with subjective evaluation. *AER*, 93(1), 216–240 ($s_6$ subjective term).
- **Chetty, R., Friedman, J. & Rockoff, J. (2014)**. Measuring the impacts of teachers. *AER*, 104(9), 2593–2679 (individual value-added under fixed pay — outcome measurement template).

nodes.content:
## Frame from personnel economics (Lazear & Oyer 2007)

truly... game theory  (incentive theory) + micro + information theory 


Quindi touches every one of the five classical dimensions:
Issue 1: Matching firms with workers. ← Further research
Issue 2:  **Organisation of work** ← lever 1.
Issue 3: **Incentives, turnover & compensation** ← lever 2.
Issue 4:  Skill development ← Further research
Issue 5:  Teamwork & worker empowerment. ← lever 2.

Quindi "extracts" information (signals) from data -> partly solves the unobservability issues generating inefficiencies and counterproductive game thoeretical responses (.... the issue in the prisoner dilemma)

Currenly I am addressing:  lever 1 and  lever 2

## The two levers

Quindi's raises productivity via two channels. Our job is to identify and estimate each one causally.


| Lever | What Quindi does | Effect channel |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Reorganisation** | Reassign each worker to their best-fit task | **Reallocation ** |
| **2. Incentives** | Apply an incentive contract $A_j$ and measure output | **Intensive margin** — same worker, same task, more effort |

These issues are linked to incomplete information: 1) in the first case you are missing some information on the "type" of the worker (productivity distribution across tasks -> conditional, stochastic markov processes ) and 2) in the second case we are missing some information on effort (extensive literature on moral hazard...)

BTW: "1. Matching firms with workers" <- missing informatin on the "type" again... 

So... is **all about information** <- the greatest is the "signal" Quindi captures (through the index) the highest the efficiency gains. 


## Deliverables
1. **Evaluation dimensions**: identify the signals $\mathbf{s}$ on which to score workers (see **Quindi Optimal Reward Formula**). "WHO" does "WHAT" in the "BEST" way. 
2. **Worker ranking**: build a composite index $R_i = \boldsymbol\beta^{*\top} \mathbf{s}_i$ using Holmström–Milgrom (1991) weights.
3. **Use the ranking**:
   - Drive the *reorganisation* lever (who goes to which task) through the evaluation dimensions
   - Drive the *incentive* lever (pay contracts of the form $A_j$) through the worker ranking

## Two research questions (two papers)
- **Paper 1 (Incentive lever)**: given task assignment, how much does contract $A_j$ change worker effort and per-task output? → **Incentives Theory** + A2–A8 alternatives.
- **Paper 2 (Reorganisation lever)**: given fixed contract, how much does AI-driven task reassignment raise firm output? → task-portfolio and assignment machinery.


## Two things to know before goign on from Lazear (2000) AER: 
1) ~44% productivity gain from switching Safelite Glass installers to a piece-rate contract. You can generate value for a company just by switching the compensation scheme! 
2) Half of the efficiency gains generated by changes in contracts are from workers self selection (issue 1), half from intensive effects

Comments: 
- Improving the compensation schemes of a company is a CLEAR edge QUINDI can have, and an established possibility in the literature
- Less research was done on generatign efficiency through channel 2. However, it reasonably makes sense that in a firm with heterogeneous workers with heterogeneous skill distributions (see model) information on the worker skill distribution can improve generalized efficiency through reallocation. 
- Considering some insights from behavioral econ: Information treatments alone may play a subtantial role. Just showing a worker its possible salary progression in the firm may generate (for free!) effort (Learning to See the World’s Opportunities: Memory, Mental Experiencing, and the Economic Lives of the Vulnerable, Ashraf et al 2024). 

## Approaches (just the ones already realized, not the full set of what i have in mind): 
**1) ABM**: simulate a firm (& calibarate to real data), ground interactions into game theory and utility theory w heterogeneous agents: 
1) Run a sensitivity analysis testing how efficiency gain deriving from quindi reorganization of work (in between [L, 100] where L is the firm starting efficiency ) affects wages, firm output and overalll efficiency.
2) run sensitivity analysis testing how incentives affect effort, cooperation, firm output, turnout etc

** 2) Causal Empirics**: self selection is a huge issue... (extra math course offered to a class... who will join..). Very foundamental econometric issue that inhibt any pubblication. 
Sell to clients as three separate mini-products: reorg-only, incentive-only, full-stack. Each arm is a legitimate offering. Famous methodology: to avoid self selection promote some clients to test freely the product. 

| Arm | Reorganisation | Incentive contract |
|---|---|---|
| **B** (0, 0) | Old assignment $\mu_0$ | Flat wage $A_0$ |
| **R** (1, 0) | **Quindi reorganises** to $\mu^*$ | Flat wage $A_0$ |
| **I** (0, 1) | Old assignment $\mu_0$ | **Quindi contract $A_j$** |
| **F** (1, 1) | **Quindi reorganises** + **Quindi contract** | |


## Strategy 2 — Staged rollout (near-best)

If 2×2 is politically hard, run in phases:

- **Phase 1** (months 1–3): random $A_j$ treatment, **assignment frozen** at $\mu_0$ → clean $\hat\tau_{\text{incent}}$.
- **Phase 2** (months 4–6): allow Quindi to reorganise → clean $\hat\tau_{\text{total}}$, then $\hat\tau_{\text{reorg}} = \hat\tau_{\text{total}} - \hat\tau_{\text{incent}}$.

**Assumption**: incentive effect stable across phases + interaction effect unidentifiable (my simulation indicicates this is a severe concern)

---

## Strategy 3 — Within-worker-within-task fixed effects (observational)

Panel data with workers doing multiple tasks over time; some clients adopt one Quindi module before the other (staggered adoption):

$$y_{ikt} \;=\; \alpha_i + \gamma_k + \delta_t + \tau_{\text{incent}} \cdot Q^{\text{incent}}_{it} + \tau_{\text{reorg}} \cdot Q^{\text{reorg}}_{it} + \varepsilon_{ikt}$$

where $y_{ikt}$ is output of worker $i$ on task $k$ at time $t$; $Q^{\text{incent}}_{it}$, $Q^{\text{reorg}}_{it}$ are module-adoption indicators.

- $\tau_{\text{incent}}$ identified from same $(i, k)$ pre vs post contract switch.
- $\tau_{\text{reorg}}$ identified from worker crossing tasks under stable contract.

nodes.title: ★ Incentives Theory — Core
nodes.content:
# Incentives Theory — Core

 TWO ISSUES: 1) EFFORT CANNOT BE OBSERVED AND  (AS A CONSEQUENCE) 2) WAGE IS PAID TO OVERALL TEAM / FIRM PRODUCTION.

## The question

**Why doesn't a worker on flat pay exert socially optimal effort?**
Two primitive frictions drive everything downstream:

1. **Effort $e$ is unobservable** (moral hazard).
2. **Individual output $s_i$ is often also unobservable** — only team/firm output is → free-riding.

nodes.title: P·Ross (1973) — Agency
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Ross, S. (1973). The economic theory of agency: the principal's problem. *AER*, 63(2), 134–139.

## Contribution
First formal statement of the **agency problem**.

## Idea
Principal delegates an action to an agent whose objectives differ. Agent has private information about the action taken.

## Result
Optimal contract must trade off **risk sharing** vs **incentive alignment**. Both parties cannot simultaneously bear efficient risk and be incentivised.

## Impact
Foundational: precedes and motivates Holmström (1979).

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

nodes.title: P·Mirrlees (1975) — Moral Hazard
nodes.content:
# Mirrlees (1975 WP; 1999 *REStud*): *The Theory of Moral Hazard and Unobservable Behaviour*

## Relationship to Ross (1973)

Ross introduces the agency problem: hidden action, conflicting objectives, incentive–insurance trade-off. Mirrlees takes this intuition and formulates it as an explicit **constrained optimisation problem**.

- Ross explains **why** agency problems exist.
- Mirrlees explains **how** the optimal second-best contract can be characterised.

## Relationship to Holmström & Milgrom (1987)

Mirrlees studies a **static** moral-hazard problem with an arbitrary wage function $w(y)$.

Holmström & Milgrom study a **continuous-time** model in which:
- output follows a Brownian motion,
- effort is chosen continuously,
- preferences are CARA,
- effort costs are quadratic.

## Core question

How should a principal design an optimal compensation contract when the agent's effort is **unobservable** and only a noisy outcome is observed?

### 1. First rigorous model of moral hazard

A principal hires a risk-averse agent.

- The agent privately chooses effort $e$.
- Effort affects the probability distribution of output,
$$y \sim F(y \mid e),$$
but is never observed directly.
- The principal observes only realised output $y$ and offers a wage schedule
$$w(y).$$

The principal chooses $w(\cdot)$ to maximise expected profit subject to two constraints:

**1. Participation / Individual rationality (PC/IR).**
$$\mathbb{E}\big[U(w(y))\big] - c(e) \;\geq\; \bar U.$$
The agent must weakly prefer accepting the contract to their outside option.

**2. Incentive compatibility (IC).**
$$e \in \arg\max_{\hat e}\;\big\{\,\mathbb{E}\big[U(w(y)) \mid \hat e\big] - c(\hat e)\,\big\}.$$
The recommended effort $e$ must be a best response by the agent.

This optimisation problem became the canonical principal–agent framework used throughout contract theory.

### 2. Characterisation of the optimal second-best contract

The optimal wage schedule depends on how *informative* each output realisation is about effort. The key object is the **likelihood score**
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial e}\log f(y \mid e),$$
which measures how much observing a particular $y$ changes the principal's belief about effort.

The first-order conditions imply that compensation should increase with this likelihood score rather than with output itself. Consequently, the optimal contract is generally **nonlinear** (try to solve for $w$ from the equation below — you need special assumptions):

$$\frac{G'(y - w(y))}{U'(w(y))} \;=\; \lambda \;+\; \mu\,\frac{f_{e}(y, e)}{f(y, e)}$$

where

- $\dfrac{G'(y - w(y))}{U'(w(y))}$ is the **shadow price of transferring one additional dollar from the principal to the agent** — the ratio of the principal's marginal utility loss to the agent's marginal utility gain.
- $\lambda$ is the Lagrange multiplier on the agent's **participation constraint**. If effort were observable ($\mu = 0$), the condition would reduce to
$$\frac{G'(y - w(y))}{U'(w(y))} = \lambda,$$
the **first-best efficient risk-sharing rule** (risk-averse agent gets a flat wage).
- $\dfrac{f_{e}(y, e)}{f(y, e)} = \dfrac{\partial \log f(y, e)}{\partial e}$ is the **likelihood score**, measuring how informative $y$ is about hidden effort. The more informative $y$, the larger the deviation from first-best risk-sharing required to provide incentives.

### 3. Why first-best is unattainable

**Step 1 — What first-best would require.**
If effort were observable, the firm could offer a **forcing contract**: pay a flat wage $w^{FB}$ iff the agent delivers $e^{FB}$; otherwise pay nothing. This delivers first-best because both goals are simultaneously reached:
- *Optimal risk-sharing* — flat wage puts all output risk on the risk-neutral firm, none on the risk-averse worker.
- *Optimal effort* — forcing the contract makes the worker exert $e^{FB}$.
 we are giving the $w^{FB}$ mecessary to lead the worker deliver $e^{FB}$!

**Step 2 — Why removing observability breaks this.**
With effort hidden, the firm *cannot verify* $e$. If it still offered the flat wage $w^{FB}$, the worker's IC becomes
$$e^{*} = \arg\max_{e}\;\mathbb{E}[U(w^{FB})] - c(e).$$
The utility term $\mathbb{E}[U(w^{FB})]$ is **constant in $e$** (wage doesn't respond to output). The worker maximises only $-c(e)$ and chooses $e^{*} = 0$. **Full shirking.** So a flat wage plus hidden effort $\Rightarrow$ zero effort.

**Step 3 — The forced compromise.**
To induce any $e > 0$, the wage **must depend on $y$**. But then two costs appear simultaneously:
1. $y = g(e) + \varepsilon$ is *noisy*, so $w(y)$ is a noisy wage. The **risk-averse** worker must be paid a **risk premium** for bearing wage variance. That's an insurance loss.
2. The wage-response to $y$ is *imperfect* (signal noise). So the induced effort under IC is generally **below** $e^{FB}$. That's an effort under-provision loss.

**Step 4 — The incentive-vs-insurance trade-off, formalised.**

| Objective | Wants | Contract feature |
|---|---|---|
| **Insurance** | Worker bears no risk | Flat wage |
| **Incentives** | Worker exerts $e^{FB}$ | Wage sensitive to $y$ |

The two objectives **cannot both be satisfied** once effort is hidden. Any feasible contract must trade one against the other. Total surplus:
$$S_{\text{2nd-best}} \;=\; S^{FB} \;-\; \underbrace{\text{effort under-provision loss}}_{\text{IC not perfectly enforceable}} \;-\; \underbrace{\text{risk premium}}_{\text{PC compensates variance}} \;<\; S^{FB}.$$

Both loss terms are strictly positive whenever the worker is risk-averse and the signal is noisy — hence first-best is **strictly unattainable**. This is Ross (1973)'s intuition, now with an explicit formal argument: it is the *joint action* of hidden effort + risk aversion + noisy signal that forces second-best.

### 4. Role of the Monotone Likelihood Ratio Property (MLRP)

**Why the FOC alone isn't enough.**
Without extra structure, the Mirrlees FOC
$$\frac{G'(y - w(y))}{U'(w(y))} = \lambda + \mu\,\frac{f_{e}(y, e)}{f(y, e)}$$
can deliver a wage schedule that is **non-monotonic in $y$** — i.e., the worker gets *paid more for mediocre output than for excellent output*.

Concrete pathology: suppose the score $f_{e}/f$ is highest at *intermediate* $y$ (because that realisation is the most informative about high effort, while both very low and very high $y$ are ambiguous). The FOC then dictates the highest wage at intermediate $y$ and *lower* wages at the extremes. Economically absurd:
- rewards mediocrity, penalises brilliance,
- gameable — worker aims for the middle,
- inconsistent with virtually every observed real-world contract.

MLRP is what rules this out.

**MLRP formally.**
For any $e_{H} > e_{L}$:
$$\frac{f(y \mid e_{H})}{f(y \mid e_{L})} \;\;\text{is non-decreasing in } y.$$
Equivalently, higher $y$ is stronger evidence of higher effort. Under MLRP, the score $\dfrac{\partial \log f(y \mid e)}{\partial e}$ is monotone-increasing in $y$.

### 5. Static optimal contracts are generally complex

A key insight: unrestricted optimal contracts need not resemble the simple compensation schemes observed in practice. The mathematically optimal $w(y)$ can be highly nonlinear, with very steep rewards or punishments in unlikely states. This complexity later motivated the search for environments in which *simple* contracts could be shown to be exactly optimal — culminating in Holmström & Milgrom (1987).

→ **BUT WE CAN EXPLORE NON LINEARITIES WITH QUINDI**

nodes.title: P·Holmström (1979) — Sufficient Statistic
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Holmström, B. (1979). Moral hazard and observability. *Bell JE*, 10(1), 74–91.

"The role of imperfect information in a principal-agent relationship subject to moral hazard is considered. A necessary and sufficient condition for imperfect information to improve on contracts based on the payoff alone is derived, and a characterization of the optimal use of such information is given"
The source of this moral hazard or incentive problem is an asymmetry of information among individuals that results because individual actions cannot be observed and hence contracted upon. A natural remedy to the problem is to invest resources into monitoring of actions and use this information in the contract. In simple situations complete monitoring may be possible, in which case a first-best solution (entailing optimal risk sharing) can be achieved by employing a forcing contract that penalizes dysfunctional behavior. Generally, however, full observation of actions is either impossible or prohibitively costly. In such situations interest centers around the use of imperfect estimators of actions in contracting.

## Contribution
Canonical PA model + **sufficient-statistic principle**.

## Idea
PA with unobservable effort $e$, noisy output $y$. Which additional signals should enter the contract?

## Result
Any signal informative about $e$ *beyond* what $y$ tells us should enter the contract. Contract $w(y, z)$ uses ALL sufficient statistics for $e$.

## Impact
**Base model** for the entire literature. Justifies A2 tournaments (peer signals), A7 subjective (manager info), A4 team pay (peer output), and multi-signal indices generally.

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

nodes.title: P·Grossman–Hart (1983) — General PA
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Grossman, S. & Hart, O. (1983). An analysis of the principal-agent problem. *Econometrica*, 51(1), 7–45.

Their innovation is to provide rigorous foundations for optimal contracting by replacing the potentially invalid first-order approach with a two-stage optimisation and establishing existence and implementability under MLRP and the Convex Distribution Function Condition (CDFC).

## Contribution
**General** PA formulation; existence conditions.

## Idea
Decompose the PA problem into (1) picking implementable effort, (2) minimising cost of inducing it. Sidesteps the invalidity of the first-order approach.

## Result
Optimal contract exists under MLRP + convex distribution function condition (CDFC).

## Impact
Mathematical foundation for HM (1987) and all subsequent PA models.

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

nodes.title: P·Holmström–Milgrom (1987) — Linear Contract (piece rates)
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1987). Aggregation and linearity in the provision of intertemporal incentives. *Econometrica*, 55(2), 303–328.

## Contribution
The paper delivers the **optimal linear contract** theorem — the workhorse of applied incentive theory. Two miracles inside: (i) *aggregation* — only cumulative output matters, and (ii) *linearity* — the optimal contract is exactly $\alpha + \beta Y_T$, not merely approximately.

---

## 1. The model

Output evolves as
$$dY_t = a_t\, dt + \sigma\, dW_t.$$

| symbol | meaning |
|---|---|
| $Y_t$ | cumulative output |
| $a_t$ | effort chosen by the agent |
| $W_t$ | standard Brownian motion |
| $\sigma$ | noise magnitude |

Observed performance = **effort + luck** — exactly Ross's hidden-action problem, now in continuous time.

## 2. Why Brownian motion?

Think of daily sales:
$$\Delta Y = \text{effort} + \text{random shocks}.$$
As the period shrinks, i.i.d. daily shocks converge to Brownian motion. So $\{W_t\}$ is simply the continuous-time limit of repeated noisy observations — nothing exotic about it.

## 3. Agent preferences

Effort is costly with quadratic cost:
$$c(a) = \tfrac{k}{2}\, a^{2}.$$
Quadratic $c$ is chosen because it produces **linear FOCs** downstream.

The agent is risk-averse with **CARA utility**:
$$U(w) = -\exp(-\rho w),$$
where $\rho$ is the coefficient of absolute risk aversion.

## 4. Why CARA?

Under CARA + Gaussian noise, the agent's expected utility collapses to the **certainty equivalent**:
$$CE = \mathbb{E}[w] \;-\; \tfrac{\rho}{2}\,\mathrm{Var}(w).$$

Instead of maximising expected utility over lotteries, the agent maximises *expected pay minus a risk penalty*. Everything becomes quadratic. This is the algebraic trick that makes the whole model tractable.

## 5. The principal's contract space

The principal can, in principle, make pay depend on the *entire path*:
$$w = f(Y_{0}, Y_{t_1}, \dots, Y_{T}),$$
for any measurable $f$. This is an **infinite-dimensional** optimisation — hopeless without a simplification.

## 6. First miracle — Aggregation

**Theorem.** Nothing is gained by paying separately for every fluctuation. Only cumulative output matters:
$$Y_{T} = \int_{0}^{T} dY_{t}.$$
Every path-dependent contract $f(Y_{0},\dots,Y_{T})$ can be replaced by one depending on $Y_{T}$ alone, without loss.

**Why.** Brownian increments are i.i.d., and with constant marginal incentives the agent's problem *separates* over time. Intermediate fluctuations carry no information about effort beyond what the cumulative outcome already reveals.

## 7. Second miracle — Linearity

Even after aggregation the contract could be
$$w = g(Y_{T})$$
for any nonlinear $g$. The theorem proves the optimum is
$$\boxed{\;w = \alpha + \beta Y_{T}\;}.$$

**Salary + constant bonus rate is exactly optimal — not approximately.** This is what makes HM 1987 the empirical workhorse: real firms almost universally use linear-in-output pay, and the theorem justifies it.

## 8. Principal's problem and $\beta^{*}$

The principal earns $Y_{T} - w$. Expected profit:
$$\mathbb{E}[Y_{T} - w] = a T - \alpha - \beta a T.$$

The participation constraint pins down $\alpha$ (firm extracts all rent above the worker's reservation utility), so only $\beta$ is a real choice variable. Substituting $a^{*} = \beta/k$ and dropping constants, the per-unit-$T$ objective is:
$$\frac{\beta}{k} - \frac{\beta^{2}}{2k} - \frac{\rho\sigma^{2}}{2}\beta^{2}.$$

FOC in $\beta$:
$$\frac{1}{k} - \frac{\beta}{k} - \rho\sigma^{2}\beta = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \beta\!\left(\rho\sigma^{2} + \tfrac{1}{k}\right) = \tfrac{1}{k}$$
$$\boxed{\;\beta^{*} = \frac{1}{1 + \rho\sigma^{2}k}\;}$$

With a general marginal-product $g'(a^{*})$ of effort on output (instead of the normalised $1$):
$$\beta^{*} = \frac{1}{1 + \rho\sigma^{2}k / g'^{\,2}}.$$

## 9. Interpretation — Ross's trade-off in closed form


| Change | Effect on $\beta^{*}$ | Intuition |
|---|---|---|
| $\rho \uparrow$ | ↓ | worker more risk-averse ⇒ costly to load risk on them |
| $\sigma^{2} \uparrow$ | ↓ | signal noisier ⇒ risk premium expensive, dial down $\beta$ |
| $k \uparrow$ | ↓ | effort more costly ⇒ weaker effort response ⇒ lower-powered incentives |
| $g' \uparrow$ | ↑ | signal more informative about effort ⇒ cheaper to incentivise |
| $\rho\sigma^{2} \to 0$ | $\to 1$ | risk-neutral worker or noiseless signal ⇒ residual claimancy, first-best |

This is Ross (1973)'s trade-off — *risk-sharing vs incentive alignment* — written in closed form. Every A-alternative in the taxonomy (piece rate, tournament, efficiency wage, team pay, subjective bonus, equity) is a *different way to design the signal $Y_T$* so this trade-off is more favourable.

---

## Impact

The universal benchmark in applied incentive theory. Every downstream contract theory paper either extends HM 1987 (multitask HM 1991, career concerns Holmström 1982, relational MacLeod 2003, tournaments Lazear–Rosen 1981) or tests it empirically (Prendergast 2002, D'Haultfœuille–Février 2020, Hossain–List 2012, Lazear 2000).

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

nodes.title: P·Holmström–Milgrom (1991) — Multitasking
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1991). Multitask principal-agent analyses: incentive contracts, asset ownership, job design. *JLEO*, 7(Special), 24–52.

## Contribution
**Multitasking** extension.

## Idea
Agent chooses effort vector $\mathbf{e}$; multiple signals $\mathbf{s}$ with noise covariance $\Sigma$; incentive weights $\boldsymbol\beta$.

## Result
$$\boldsymbol\beta^* = (I + \rho C \Sigma)^{-1} \mathbf{g}'$$
If one task cannot be measured ($\beta_j = 0$), agent sets $e_j = 0$; firm must **dampen ALL** $\beta_k$ to preserve balance.

## Impact
**F2 multitasking**. Direct foundation for our Quindi Optimal formula.

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

nodes.title: P·Lazear–Rosen (1981) — Tournaments
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Lazear, E. & Rosen, S. (1981). Rank-order tournaments as optimum labor contracts. *JPE*, 89(5), 841–864.

## Contribution
Pay by *rank*, not by cardinal output. Under risk-neutrality this contract *implements first-best effort exactly* — unlike HM 1987's linear contract, which only achieves $\beta^{*} < 1$.

## Setup

Two workers, indexed $i, j$. Each produces observable output $y = \mu(e) + \varepsilon$ with i.i.d. noise $\varepsilon \sim F$. Effort cost is quadratic, $c(e) = \tfrac{1}{2}ke^{2}$. Workers are risk-neutral (this is what makes the miracle work; §III relaxes it). The firm ranks $y_i, y_j$ and pays winner $w_H$, loser $w_L$. Only the *spread* $\Delta = w_H - w_L$ matters for incentives.

## Step 1 — worker's win probability

Worker $i$ wins iff $y_i > y_j$, equivalently $\mu(e_i) - \mu(e_j) > \varepsilon_j - \varepsilon_i$. Let $\xi = \varepsilon_j - \varepsilon_i$ with density $G(\cdot)$. Then
$$P_i^{\text{win}}(e_i, e_j) = \Pr\!\big(\xi < \mu(e_i)-\mu(e_j)\big).$$

Key observation: $\xi$ is *common-shock-free*. Any market or weather shock $\eta$ that hits both workers cancels in the difference. This is the tournament's headline advantage over piece rates (LR 1981 §II).

## Step 2 — worker's IC

$\mathbb E[U_i] = w_L + \Delta \cdot P_i^{\text{win}}(e_i, e_j) - c(e_i)$. Taking the FOC in $e_i$:
$$\Delta \cdot \mu'(e_i) \cdot G\!\big(\mu(e_i)-\mu(e_j)\big) = c'(e_i).$$
In the symmetric Nash equilibrium $e_i = e_j = e^{*}$, the density is evaluated at zero:
$$\boxed{\;\Delta \cdot \mu'(e^{*}) \cdot G(0) = c'(e^{*})\;}\quad\text{(IC)}.$$

With Gaussian noise $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal N(0,\sigma^{2})$, $\xi \sim \mathcal N(0, 2\sigma^{2})$ so $G(0) = 1/\sqrt{4\pi\sigma^{2}}$. Under $\mu(e)=e$ and quadratic cost this solves to
$$e^{*} = \frac{\Delta}{k\sigma\sqrt{4\pi}}.$$

## Step 3 — firm's problem

Two constraints on $(w_L, \Delta)$. Participation: symmetry means each worker wins with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, so expected wage is $w_L + \Delta/2$; PC binds at $w_L + \tfrac{1}{2}\Delta - c(e^{*}) = \bar U$. Incentive-compatibility: the IC above.

Expected profit across the two workers is
$$\Pi = 2\mu(e^{*}) - (2w_L + \Delta).$$
Substituting $w_L$ from PC:
$$\Pi = 2\mu(e^{*}) - 2c(e^{*}) - 2\bar U.$$

Notice that $\Delta$ has dropped out of the firm's objective. The firm now maximises *joint surplus* $\mu(e) - c(e)$, evaluated at whatever effort $\Delta$ induces through IC.

## Step 4 — the miracle: first-best

Since the firm can pick any effort level by adjusting $\Delta$ (IC is a continuous map $\Delta \mapsto e^{*}$) and its objective is unconstrained joint surplus, the optimum is where $\mu'(e^{*}) = c'(e^{*})$ — the first-best condition. Substituting back into IC:
$$\boxed{\;\Delta^{*} = \frac{1}{G(0)} = 2\sigma\sqrt{\pi}\;}\quad(\text{Gaussian noise, }\mu(e)=e).$$

*Tournaments implement first-best under risk-neutrality.* HM 1987's linear contract can never do this — its risk premium keeps $\beta^{*} < 1$ so long as $\rho\sigma^{2} > 0$. Here we hit $e^{FB}$ exactly.

## Comparative statics

Effort rises linearly in the prize spread and falls with noise, cost curvature, and (in the $N$-worker extension) team size. The *optimal* spread $\Delta^{*}$ rises with noise (more noise flattens the win-probability curve, so a bigger prize is needed to keep the marginal incentive at its first-best level) and with $N$ (harder to rank first when more competitors), but is independent of $k$ (the first-best target simply shifts to a lower effort).

## Where the miracle fails

Four assumptions in Step 4 are load-bearing, and each has been shown to break the first-best result:

**Homogeneous peers.** If workers differ in $k_i$ or $\bar U_i$, tournaments select adversely (Rosen 1986) — high-cost workers self-select out, low-cost workers extract rents, and effort is no longer first-best.

**No sabotage.** Payoff depends on relative rank, so ruining a rival is as valuable as improving yourself (Chan-Zheng 2011, Chowdhury-Gürtler 2015). Sabotage equilibria dominate the pure-effort equilibrium and predict systematically lower total surplus than piece rates. This is F5 in the pathology list.

**Perfect common-shock cancellation.** In practice, shocks decompose into a common and an idiosyncratic component; only the common part cancels in $\xi$. Tournaments still bear idiosyncratic risk, and lose to piece rates when the idiosyncratic share dominates.

**Risk neutrality.** Under CARA workers, a risk-premium term re-enters the FOC. Section III of LR 1981 derives this: $\Delta^{*}$ falls, first-best is no longer attainable, and the tournament-vs-piece-rate comparison becomes ambiguous (Green-Stokey 1983 gives the sharp comparison — piece rates dominate for small noise, tournaments dominate for large noise).

## Impact

Grounds contract family A2 in the taxonomy and the entire promotion-contest / sales-tournament / CEO-succession literature. Empirical tests: Ehrenberg-Bognanno (1990) on PGA golf tournaments; Bandiera-Barankay-Rasul (2005) on relative-vs-piece incentives with fruit-pickers; Casas-Arce-Martínez-Jerez (2009) on sales-force tournaments; Frederiksen-Halliday-Koch (2017) on hospital management.

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

nodes.title: P·Lazear (1979) — Deferred Comp
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Lazear, E. (1979). Why is there mandatory retirement? *JPE*, 87(6), 1261–1284.

## Contribution
Theory of **back-loaded pay** as an incentive device.

## Idea
Set wage below MPL early, above MPL late. Shirking (if detected) forfeits future rents.

## Result
Worker's participation requires future rent > shirking gain today. Mandatory retirement needed to prevent perpetual over-payment.

## Impact
**A5 Deferred Compensation**. Explains seniority wage profiles, defined-benefit pensions, tenure track.

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

nodes.title: P·Holmström (1982) — Career Concerns
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Holmström, B. (1982 working paper; 1999 *REStud* 66(1), 169–182). Managerial incentive problems: a dynamic perspective.

## Contribution
**Career concerns**: implicit incentives via market reputation. Also introduces **yardstick** peer benchmarks.

## Idea
Worker's ability $\theta$ unknown to labor market. Signal $s_t = \theta + e_t + \varepsilon_t$. Market Bayes-updates; future wage $\propto \mathbb{E}[\theta \mid s_{1:t}]$.

## Result
Even with $\beta = 0$ today, worker exerts $e_t > 0$ to signal high $\theta$. Effort declines toward retirement (horizon effect).

## Impact
**A6 Career Concerns**. Also the **yardstick** fix for **F3 ratchet** (peer-indexed quotas).

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

nodes.title: P·Fama (1980) — Implicit Incentives
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Fama, E. (1980). Agency problems and the theory of the firm. *JPE*, 88(2), 288–307.

## Contribution
**Implicit incentives via managerial labor market**.

## Idea
Even without explicit performance contracts, market reputation disciplines managers. Managerial labor market prices past performance directly.

## Result
Formal incentive contracts are less crucial than reputational ones. Firm's board is redundant if market pricing is efficient.

## Impact
**A6 Career Concerns** (alongside Holmström 1982). Motivates CEO market discipline.

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

nodes.title: P·Shapiro–Stiglitz (1984) — Efficiency Wage
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Shapiro, C. & Stiglitz, J. (1984). Equilibrium unemployment as a worker discipline device. *AER*, 74(3), 433–444.

## Contribution
**Efficiency-wage** theory + involuntary unemployment.

## Idea
Firm pays $w > w^{MC}$; monitors with probability $q$; dismisses on detected shirking.

## Result
**No-shirking condition**:
$$w - w^{MC} \geq \frac{c(e)(1-\delta)}{q\delta}$$
Involuntary unemployment sustains the punishment: dismissal must be costly.

## Impact
**A3 Efficiency Wage**. Also explains persistent unemployment.

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

nodes.title: P·Baker–Gibbons–Murphy (1994) — Subjective
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Baker, G., Gibbons, R. & Murphy, K. J. (1994). Subjective performance measures in optimal incentive contracts. *QJE*, 109(4), 1125–1156.

## Contribution
Optimal contract combining **objective + subjective** measures.

## Idea
Objective signal $y$ is noisy or gameable; subjective rating $m$ is manager's private info. Contract uses both.

## Result
Optimal weights vary **inversely with variance and gameability** of each. Subjective term corrects gaming of $y$; objective term disciplines manager.

## Impact
**A7 Subjective Evaluation**. Justifies hybrid pay systems ubiquitous in corporate practice.

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

nodes.title: P·MacLeod (2003) — Relational Contracts
nodes.content:
**Ref.** MacLeod, W. B. (2003). Optimal contracting with subjective evaluation. *AER*, 93(1), 216–240.

## Contribution
**Relational-contract** foundation for subjective evaluation.

## Idea
Manager's rating is private; workers can only trust it if the manager's reputation for fairness is sustained.

## Result
Relational contract sustains subjective bonus iff discount $\delta$ is high enough (repeated game). Reneging destroys equilibrium — one-shot subjective evaluation collapses.

## Impact
**A7 Subjective**. Explains why subjective bonuses work in long-tenure firms and fail in high-turnover ones.

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

nodes.title: P·Jensen–Meckling (1976) — Agency Costs
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Jensen, M. & Meckling, W. (1976). Theory of the firm: managerial behavior, agency costs and ownership structure. *JFE*, 3(4), 305–360.

## Contribution
Foundational **agency-cost** framework applied to ownership.

## Idea
Managers with < 100% ownership divert firm resources (perks, shirking). Ownership share $\phi$ reduces divergence.

## Result
**Agency cost** = deadweight loss from manager–shareholder objective divergence. Increasing $\phi$ trades off manager alignment vs risk-sharing.

## Impact
**A8 Ownership / Equity**. Founding paper of corporate-governance economics.

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

nodes.title: P·Hansmann (1996) — Ownership of Enterprise
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Hansmann, H. (1996). *The Ownership of Enterprise*. Harvard University Press.

## Contribution
Book-length theory of **who should own firms**.

## Idea
Assign ownership to the input-supplier whose contributions are hardest to contract on ex-ante. Whoever bears the residual risk best is the efficient owner.

## Result
Explains investor-owned firms, worker cooperatives, consumer cooperatives, mutuals as efficient solutions in different environments.

## Impact
**A8 Ownership**. Theoretical rationale for employee ownership when human capital is dominant.

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

nodes.title: P·Kandel–Lazear (1992) — Peer Pressure
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Kandel, E. & Lazear, E. (1992). Peer pressure and partnerships. *JPE*, 100(4), 801–817.

## Contribution
**Peer pressure** as a supplement to team pay.

## Idea
In small teams under team pay, peer pressure $\psi$ raises effective cost of shirking. Free-rider ($\propto 1/N$) offset by peer observability.

## Result
Optimal team size trades off free-riding vs peer monitoring. Small $N$ sustains cooperation; large $N$ needs formal supervision.

## Impact
**A4 Team Pay**. Explains professional partnerships (law, medicine, consulting).

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

nodes.title: P·Gibbons (1987) — Ratchet
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Gibbons, R. (1987). Piece-rate incentive schemes. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 5(4), 413–429.

## Contribution
Formalizes the **ratchet effect**.

## Idea
Two periods. Firm updates target based on period-1 output. Rational worker under-produces in $t=1$ to keep $t=2$ target low.

## Result
$$e_1^* < e^{\text{one-shot}}$$
Strategic hiding is welfare-reducing. Worse when firm cannot commit to future quotas.

## Impact
**F3 Ratchet Effect**. Motivates yardstick competition (Holmström 1982; Shleifer 1985).

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

nodes.title: P·Hamilton–Nickerson–Owan (2003) — Cooperation
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Hamilton, B., Nickerson, J. & Owan, H. (2003). Team incentives and worker heterogeneity. *JPE*, 111(3), 465–497.

## Contribution
Empirical evidence of **cooperation collapse** under piece rates.

## Idea
Garment plant switched from team pay to individual piece rates. Detailed data before and after.

## Result
**Total output FELL** despite individual effort rising. Workers stopped teaching, helping, covering.

## Impact
**F5 Cooperation Collapse**. Empirical evidence that peer help is a *priced* good under team pay and a *free* good under piece rates.

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

nodes.title: P·Lazear (2000) — Safelite
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Lazear, E. (2000). Performance pay and productivity. *AER*, 90(5), 1346–1361.

## Contribution
The **Safelite Auto Glass** field experiment.

## Idea
Company switched from hourly wages to per-windshield piece rate over 19 months. Rich individual-level data.

## Result
**+44% productivity gain.** Decomposition:
- ~**½ effort** response;
- ~**½ sorting**: high-productivity workers self-selected into piece-rate firm.

## Impact
**A1 Piece Rate** and **A9 Selection**. THE most-cited empirical study on high-powered incentives.

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

nodes.title: P·Prendergast (1999) — Survey
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Prendergast, C. (1999). The provision of incentives in firms. *JEL*, 37(1), 7–63.

## Contribution
**Comprehensive survey** of the incentives literature.

## Idea
Review theoretical and empirical evidence on incentive contracts. Confront theory with actual firm practice.

## Result
Explicit piece rates are **rare** in observed data. Most workers on fixed wages + subjective bonuses. Risk-incentive tradeoff empirically weaker than theory predicts (Prendergast 2002).

## Impact
Reality-check on the whole literature. Motivates A3 (fixed wage + efficiency wage) and A7 (subjective) as empirically dominant.

→ Anchor: **Incentives Theory Core**

trash.title: A5. Deferred Compensation / Seniority Pay (Lazear 1979, 1981)
trash.content:
**Signal**: tenure. Pay < marginal product early, > marginal product late.

**Solves**
- Bonds worker to firm — being fired for shirking forfeits back-loaded pay.
- Long horizon dampens the ratchet incentive (F3): giving up short-run output for long-run tenure.
- Long horizon dampens Goodhart bunching (F6): quarter-end games matter less if 30-year payoff dominates.
- Solves moral hazard when short-run output isn't measurable but reputation shapes retention.

**Breaks**
- Requires credible commitment from firm not to fire senior workers arbitrarily.
- Creates incentives for mandatory retirement (Lazear 1979).
- Weakens mobility — inefficient if outside options shift.

**Use when**: firm-specific human capital matters, output hard to measure period-by-period, firm has commitment techno

trash.title: A6. Career Concerns / Implicit Incentives (Fama 1980; Holmström 1982)
trash.content:
**Signal**: your *future outside wage*, priced by the labor market from observed output.

**Solves**
- Market averages many noisy signals over time → attacks measurement noise (F1).
- Naturally captures multidimensional output — market cares about overall ability, not one metric (F2).
- Removes the ratchet (F3): market has no incentive to raise your standard if you produce more.
- Continuous market pricing → no threshold to bunch at (F6).

**Breaks**
- Horizon effect: incentive weakens toward retirement (Gibbons–Murphy 1992).
- Effort tilts to visible, market-legible activities → private-value tasks under-provided.
- Requires market observability of individual output.

**Use when**: high-visibility labor markets (CEOs, academics, professional services).
